parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Variation
parent.overview: The QGD with 3.Nc3 develops the knight and adds pressure on d5. The usual continuation is 3...Nf6, after which White chooses 4.Bg5 (pin; Black replies Orthodox 4...Be7, Cambridge Springs, Tartakower ...b6 or Lasker ...Ne4), 4.Nf3 or the Exchange 4.cxd5. Black holds d5 with ...e6, which gives a bulletproof centre but locks the c8 bishop; Black frees the game with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Bb7. White's main plans are the minority attack (b4-b5 against c6) in Exchange structures, or central play with e4. Play is slow and technical rather than tactical, with a strong reputation for soundness, and the Cambridge Springs is the one trappy tactical sub-line.

parent.name: Vienna Game
parent.overview: White develops the queen's knight before the king's knight, protecting e4 and adding a second guard of d5, and keeps the f-pawn free. That flexibility is the point: White can later play f4 for a delayed King's Gambit (the Vienna Gambit), develop the bishop with 3.Bc4 for an Italian or Bishop's Opening structure (with the Qg4 raid against ...Bc5 and the Frankenstein-Dracula after ...Nxe4), or fianchetto with 3.g3 for a quieter game. Black usually answers 2...Nf6 (the Falkbeer, about 60 percent in one source) or 2...Nc6, and the standard equaliser is a timely ...d5. Theory leaves the opening objectively equal, with little elite use but a lot of club use; it is a surprise weapon that avoids the heavily prepared Spanish and Italian lines. The root is a family, so its character depends on White's third move.

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Normal Defense
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Black answers 3.Nc3 with the natural 3...Nf6, defending d5 and eyeing e4. This is a crossroads in which White chooses between 4.Bg5 (the pin and the classical Orthodox, Lasker, Tartakower and Cambridge Springs lines), 4.cxd5 (the Exchange and Carlsbad structure, dominant at 2500 level) and 4.Nf3, which keeps options open and lets Black pick a QGD, Ragozin (...Bb4) or Semi-Slav (...c6) set-up (s1, s4). The QGD systems are solid with straightforward plans: ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O against most lines, and the ...c5 break (s2). White's typical plans are the minority attack and e4 expansion (s1). The Semi-Slav moves 4.Nf3 c6 5.Bg5 (Botvinnik) are outside the QGD in character, very forcing (s4). The root as a whole is the Orthodox QGD family and its transpositions. The site's current text for this root is a copy of the parent QGD text.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.

parent.name: Bishop's Opening: Berlin Defense
parent.overview: White's bishop on c4 eyes f7 and Black answers with 2...Nf6, hitting e4 at once. White's standard reply is 3.d3 (defending e4 and keeping f4 and later c3/d4 available); 3.Nc3 transposes to a Vienna Game and 3.Nf3 to the Italian or Two Knights. Black usually continues 3...c6 (Paulsen) planning ...d5 to hit the bishop with tempo, or 3...Nc6/...Bc5 reaching the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo. Most play is therefore a calm Italian-style game with a small White space edge. Sharper options exist but are rare: 3.d4 (Urusov Gambit, a pawn for attack) and 3.f4 (Greco Gambit, transposing to the Bishop's Gambit after ...exf4). Nick de Firmian's verdict is that the Berlin leads to equality with best play.

parent.name: Italian Game
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 aiming at f7 and prepares to take the centre with c3 and d4 or, more quietly, d3 (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's set-up, 3...Nf6 (Two Knights) invites sharper play, and 3...Be7 (Hungarian) is passive and solid (own understanding for the last). Today's main practical line is the Giuoco Pianissimo with c3, d3 and slow manoeuvring, which became fashionable in the 1980s-2000s and again in the 21st century as a way to avoid the Berlin (s1). The older 4.c3 and d4 lines and the Evans Gambit are sharper (s1). It is fundamentally sound with modest winning chances (s1). It is described as accessible to beginners yet used by Giri, So and Vachier-Lagrave (s3).

parent.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
parent.overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.
